subject: Piecewise exponential hazard model with autoregressive prior

messages.author: 4031b4611d7c812a
messages.subject: Piecewise exponential hazard model with autoregressive prior
parts:
Hi all,

My name is Peter. I would like to know whether INLA can be used to fit piecewise exponential hazard model with autoregressive prior of order 1. I have fitted such model using MCMC which is implemented using RJags (the code is given in the attached document [rjags piecewise rho 0.95.txt] and the Rjags results [rjags piecewise with rho 0.95.txt]) with age as the only covariate (the covariate has been centred by subtracting its mean from each actual observation). In this model, I would want the hazards in the intervals that are closely together should be likely similar. The mathematical details on how to construct an autoregressive prior of order 1 for this model is given in piecewise model INLAforum.pdf (section 1.1.3), together with the rest of the details on the piecewise model that I wish to fit. The dataset used for RJags is also attached (file name: snlgdatafull.txt).

To create / discretise the time axis into ten intervals (cut off points used to construct the intervals are 0.105, 0.223, 0.357, 0.511, 0.693, 0.916, 1.204, 1.609, 2.303), piecewiseirfan function was used (given in the rjags piecewise rho 0.95.txt).

I have attempted to fit such model using INLA but my effort was unsuccessful (the RINLA commands and results obtained are given in the text files and the dataset for INLA is datasetINLA.txt).  Hence, I hope someone can point me towards the right direction. Cheers.


Peter

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Piecewise exponential hazard model with autoregressive prior
parts:
Hi & thanks for your email.

This is quite interesting, and there is no direct support as now I
*think* (unless you can make use of the 'coxph' expansion that exists
(see ?inla.coxph). To me it looks like many of the details are the same
(see the Martino et al paper in Scand J of Stat, in 2011 or so).

In short, the dataframe has to be expanded and converted into an
'exponential' observations, where all the likelihood contributions

lambda * exp(- ... * lambda)
exp(-... * lambda)

can be represented a an observed or cencored exponential distribution,
or a Poisson distribtion (see the note for the Poisson likelihood,
where it states that ``This likelihood also accept E = 0 and in this
case log(E) is defined to be 0.'' This is used for the LGCP, as was
added for this case to be smooth.

So, with an expansion of the data.frame you should be able to do this.
I am a little unsure about the connection with the coxph models that
there is (like using log hazard model a RW2 instead of RW1), but maybe
Sara.M knows more...

Best
H

messages.author: 8be293492d512f32
messages.subject: Re: Piecewise exponential hazard model with autoregressive prior
parts:
Hi Peter
I think this will do what you want 

INLAdata<-read.table("Downloads/dataINLA.txt",header=TRUE)
cutscoxph=c(0,0.105, 0.223, 0.357, 0.511, 0.693, 0.916, 1.204, 1.609,
2.303, 5)
y.surv = inla.surv(INLAdata$t, INLAdata$status)
p = inla.coxph(y.surv ~ -1 + int + age, 
                data = list(y.surv = y.surv, 
                            int = rep(1,dim(INLAdata)[1]),
                            age = INLAdata$age),
                control.hazard = list(cutpoints = cutscoxph)
                )
new.data = data.frame(y = p$data$E..coxph,
                       delta = p$data$y..coxph,
                       age = p$data$age,
                       interval = p$data$baseline.hazard.idx)
formula = inla.surv(y,delta) ~ f(interval, model = "rw1") + age
res = inla(formula, data = new.data, family = "exponential.surv")

bests
sara

parts:
Hi all,

Thank you  for your kind replies and the inla.coxph code. I really appreciate it. The code works well and is partially what I require for my piecewise model. By the way, I would also like to know whether INLA can accommodate  a prior structure that makes that makes the hazard parameters in neighbouring intervals to be correlated? The mathematical details are given in section 1.1.3 of the uploaded pdf document. I implemented it in rjags using the following model specification:


modelstringfull="
model 
{
  for (i in 1:3496)
  {
  is.cen[i]~dinterval(t[i], t.cen[i])
  
  t[i]~dexp(lambda.whole[i]) 
  
  lambda.whole[i]<-exp(beta0[perj[i]]+beta.age[perj[i]]*(age[patients[i]])) 
  }
  
 
  #---------------------------------------------
  #Priors for age and intercept FOR THE1st INTERVAL (J=1)
  #---------------------------------------------
  
  beta0[1]~dnorm(-1.5,6.25) 
  
  beta.age[1]~dnorm(0.04,1111.1)
  
  #---------------------------------------------------
  #DYNAMIC PART A: INTERCEPT AND CONTINUOUS COVARIATES
  #----------------------------------------------------
  
  p0.e<-6.25
  p.age.e<-1111.1
  
  #------------------------------------------------------------------
  # PRIOR FOR 2ND INTERVAL (J=2) UNTIL THE (J=10) INTERVAL
  #-------------------------------------------------------------------
  
  for (j in 2:10)
  {                   
  beta0m[j]<-beta0[j-1]
  beta0[j]~dnorm(beta0m[j],p0.e)
  
  beta.agem[j]<-beta.age[j-1]
  beta.age[j]~dnorm(beta.agem[j],p.age.e)
  }
}
"

messages.author: b5df203d4c72831c
messages.subject: Re: Piecewise exponential hazard model with autoregressive prior
parts:
Hi Sara,

Thanks for your reply. Yes, if possible I would like to make the effect of age to be time dependent too. For MCMC, I specified the autoregressive (1) prior structure for the age covariate (in the jags model) so that the effect of age covariate in one time interval (i.e.time interval = j) is influenced by its effect in the preceding interval (time interval = j-1). To do this rjags, I firstly specified the prior values for beta0 and beta.age for the first interval:

 #---------------------------------------------
  #Priors for age and intercept FOR THE 1st INTERVAL (J=1)
Then, for the 2nd interval (J=2) until the 10th interval (J=10), the priors are specified so that the prior mean for interval J is dependent on the prior mean of the preceding interval (J-1)

for (j in 2:10)
  {                   
  beta0m[j]<-beta0[j-1]
  beta0[j]~dnorm(beta0m[j],p0.e)
  
  beta.agem[j]<-beta.age[j-1]
  beta.age[j]~dnorm(beta.agem[j],p.age.e)
  }
}
"

The results obtained are as presented in the my previous post. Thanks and I really appreciate your help. All the best. Cheers.

Kind regards,
Peter.
